 Question of the Day 
 How many ‘ghost students’ were found collecting federal student aid?
 Answer: More than 830,000.
 October 30, 2026 •  
 Helaina Dahl 
 Facebook 
 LinkedIn 
 Twitter 
 Print 
 Email 
 CC BY-SA 2.0 
 By Helaina Dahl.
 The federal Department of Justice (DOJ) has uncovered a large-scale scheme that allegedly used AI to fraudulently collect federal student aid funds.
How it starts, apparently, is with bad actors purchasing people’s personally identifiable information and using it to fill out Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) forms. If an application is accepted, the money first goes to the university chosen, but then any extra funds flow into the fraudulent bank account. To keep up the ruse, AI is used to fill out coursework and applications — it can even make it appear as if they are a student attending virtual class.
These ghost student schemes have produced almost $130 million in total losses, and the person whose data was stolen often doesn’t know it happened until the government comes to collect on loans years later.
 A possible solution for colleges and universities to crack down on ghost student fraud would be to add fees. But critics suggest this could eventually become a barrier for real students attempting to get their education. Students are expected to have government-issued IDs on hand while filling out FAFSA applications, but with recent fraud attempts, some students could be, and have been, flagged accidentally.
